issues.legal_issue: The characterization of a transaction as an adventure in the nature of trade is a mixed question of law and fact that may be challenged in a statutory tax reference.
material_facts: The Tribunal classified the purchase of an industrial property and its subsequent partial sale as an adventure in the nature of trade.
The reference asked whether the purchase was part of a profit-making scheme or an adventure in the nature of trade.
issues.conclusion: The Tribunal must find the primary evidentiary facts and apply the legal meaning of the statutory expression; its decision on that mixed question is open to challenge under section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(4) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, the statutory expression “adventure in the nature of trade” requires applying the legal principles associated with trade to primary facts. Section 66(1) permits a challenge in a reference to a decision on this mixed question. The Court relied on Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax.

predicates.tax_reference_from_tribunal: A party brings a statutory tax reference challenging the Tribunal’s decision.
predicates.transaction_classification_requires_prim: The classification of the transaction depends on primary evidentiary facts and the application of a legal standard.

issues.definition: When a tax reference challenges a Tribunal’s classification that depends on both primary facts and a legal standard, the classification is reviewable as a mixed question of law and fact.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a property purchase and resale is an adventure in the nature of trade depends on the total effect of the relevant facts and circumstances, and the transaction here was part of a profit-making scheme.
material_facts: The firm purchased an industrial factory and its associated property using borrowed money and invested little of its own funds.
The income from the property was about one-sixth of the interest payable on the borrowed money.
The firm began selling part of the property within about three months of the purchase.
It used sale proceeds to pay purchase debts and amounts due to the government, and had sold substantial property while still owing money.
The evidence did not establish that the firm bought the factory to establish a cycle factory or another industry.
issues.conclusion: Considering the total effect of the established facts, the purchase and resale of the property was an adventure in the nature of trade and part of a profit-making scheme; the resulting profit was assessable.
issues.legal_principle: The meaning of “business” in section 2(4) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, includes an adventure in the nature of trade; the equivalent provisions of the Hyderabad Income Tax Act also applied to one assessment year. Whether a transaction falls within that expression depends on the total impression and effect of all relevant facts, not an abstract formula. A land transaction is not, without more, presumed to be an adventure in the nature of trade. The Court applied Venkataswami Naidu & Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax and referred to Californian Copper Syndicate v. Harris, Martin v. Lowry, Rutledge v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Fraser, Leeming v. Jones, Saroj Kumar Mazumdar v. Commissioner of Income-tax, and Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Reinhold.

rule.if: taxable_profit_classification_case and property_purchased_and_partly_resold and purchase_financed_by_borrowing and own_funds_inadequate_for_permanent_investment and property_yield_far_below_financing_cost and resale_began_soon_after_purchase and sale_proceeds_used_to_repay_debts and no_evidence_established_intended_industrial_use

predicates.taxable_profit_classification_case: A tax proceeding concerns whether profit from purchasing and reselling an asset is taxable as business profit.
predicates.property_purchased_and_partly_resold: The taxpayer bought property and later sold part of it.
predicates.purchase_financed_by_borrowing: The taxpayer used borrowed money to finance the purchase.
predicates.own_funds_inadequate_for_permanent_inves: The taxpayer lacked sufficient own financial resources to make the purchase as a permanent investment.
predicates.property_yield_far_below_financing_cost: The income from the property was substantially lower than the cost of financing its purchase.
predicates.resale_began_soon_after_purchase: The taxpayer began reselling part of the property shortly after acquiring it.
predicates.sale_proceeds_used_to_repay_debts: The taxpayer used proceeds from sales to discharge purchase-related debts or amounts due to the seller.
predicates.no_evidence_established_intended_industr: The evidence did not establish that the taxpayer acquired the property to use it for an intended industrial purpose.

issues.definition: In a tax proceeding about profit on resale, when a taxpayer buys and partly resells property using borrowing, lacks funds for permanent investment, earns far less from the property than the financing costs, begins resale soon after purchase, uses proceeds to repay debts, and has no evidence establishing intended industrial use, the transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade and the resulting profit is assessable.

issues.legal_issue: A Tribunal preparing a statement of case for a tax reference must set out the relevant arguments, authorities, statutory provisions, facts, and findings clearly enough for the reviewing court to decide the referred question.
material_facts: The Tribunal’s statement of case did not adequately describe the parties’ arguments or the Tribunal’s findings.
The statement required the High Court or Supreme Court to deduce findings or collect facts from numerous documents in the record.
issues.conclusion: The Tribunal’s statement of case was unsatisfactory; a statement of case must clearly and precisely set out the relevant arguments, authorities or statutory provisions, an intelligible summary of the facts, and the Tribunal’s conclusions and findings.
issues.legal_principle: A statement of case in a statutory tax reference is not merely a copy of the order sheet. It must set out the matters necessary to determine the referred question, including the relevant arguments, authorities or statutory provisions, facts, and clear conclusions and findings; the reviewing court should not be left to reconstruct them from the record.

predicates.tax_reference_requires_statement_of_case: A tax proceeding requires the Tribunal to prepare a statement of case for a reviewing court.
predicates.statement_omits_relevant_arguments_or_fa: The Tribunal’s statement leaves out relevant arguments, an intelligible account of the facts, or clear findings, requiring the reviewing court to reconstruct them from the record.

issues.definition: When a tax reference requires a statement of case and that statement omits relevant arguments, facts, or clear findings, the Tribunal must provide a complete and clear statement of case.
